ai.subject: Pathology
ai.summary: Immune Thrombocytopenic Purpura (ITP) is an acquired autoimmune disorder where IgG antibodies target platelet glycoproteins, leading to rapid splenic destruction and low platelet counts. Diagnosis rests on isolated thrombocytopenia after excluding other causes.

sections.p: ITP is defined by a platelet count <100 × 10⁹/L with no other hematologic or systemic cause. Diagnosis is one of exclusion, requiring a thorough history, physical exam, and basic labs.
b: Platelet count <100 × 10⁹/L
Normal hemoglobin and white cell count
Absence of schistocytes or other peripheral smear abnormalities

t.a: Complete blood count with peripheral smear
t.b: Does the patient have isolated thrombocytopenia? → Confirms the key laboratory feature; normal smear supports ITP.
Are secondary infections present? → Positive results shift diagnosis to secondary ITP.
Is marrow production adequate? → Normal or increased megakaryocytes support peripheral destruction; low production suggests other marrow disease.

sections.p: Severity guides treatment urgency. The most used system grades bleeding risk rather than platelet count alone.
b: Mild: platelet >30 × 10⁹/L, no bleeding
Moderate: 10‑30 × 10⁹/L, minor mucosal bleeding
Severe: <10 × 10⁹/L or life‑threatening bleed

sections.p: ITP can be primary (idiopathic) or secondary to infections, drugs, or systemic diseases. In low‑resource settings, certain infections are common triggers.
b: Primary autoimmune ITP (most common in children and young adults)
HIV infection
Hepatitis C
Tuberculosis
Malaria
Helicobacter pylori
Drug‑induced (e.g., quinine, sulfonamides, antiepileptics)
Systemic lupus erythematosus

sections.p: Patients often notice easy bruising, petechiae, or mucosal bleeding. Severe thrombocytopenia can cause epistaxis, gum bleed, or intracranial hemorrhage.
b: Petechiae on lower limbs
Purpura after minor trauma
Mucosal bleeding (nose, gums)
Rare: intracranial bleed with headache or neurological change

sections.p: Focused tests confirm isolated thrombocytopenia, rule out mimics, and identify treatable secondary causes.

t.b: What is the severity? → Guides urgency of therapy; <10 × 10⁹/L is high‑risk.
Are platelets reduced without abnormal cells? → Normal smear supports peripheral destruction; schistocytes suggest TMA.
Is there a coagulopathy? → Normal results help exclude DIC.
Is there a secondary infection? → Positive tests change management to treat underlying disease.
Is H. pylori present? → Eradication can improve platelet counts in some adults.

sections.p: Bleeding complications are the main danger; severe thrombocytopenia can lead to intracranial hemorrhage, especially in children.
b: Platelets <10 × 10⁹/L
Unexplained severe headache or neurological deficit
Persistent or worsening mucosal bleed despite therapy

sections.p: Treat the underlying trigger first, then control platelet destruction. First‑line agents aim to raise platelets quickly while avoiding excessive immunosuppression.
b: Treat secondary cause (e.g., start antiretroviral therapy for HIV)
Corticosteroids (prednisone or dexamethasone) – reduce antibody production
Intravenous immunoglobulin (IVIG) – blocks Fc receptors, useful for rapid rise or before surgery
Anti‑D immunoglobulin (in Rh‑positive, non‑splenectomized) – similar mechanism to IVIG
Avoid unnecessary platelet transfusion unless life‑threatening bleed

sections.p: Monitor platelet trends and bleeding signs. Education on avoiding trauma and NSAIDs reduces bleed risk. Relapse is common; long‑term follow‑up is essential.
b: Check platelet count weekly until stable, then monthly
Advise patients to seek care for any new bruising, epistaxis, or headache
Vaccinate against encapsulated organisms if splenectomy is considered

sections.p: Several conditions mimic ITP by causing low platelets or similar skin findings.
b: Thrombotic thrombocytopenic purpura – has schistocytes, neurologic changes, renal involvement
Dengue fever – fever, leukopenia, elevated liver enzymes
Aplastic anemia – pancytopenia, hypocellular marrow
Leukemia – blasts on smear, systemic symptoms

sections.p: Certain labs may appear normal despite active disease, leading to false reassurance.
b: Platelet count can transiently rise after IVIG, masking ongoing destruction
Peripheral smear may look normal even when antibodies are present
Coagulation tests are normal in ITP, but DIC can coexist in severe infections

whenToSeekHelp: Sudden severe headache or neurological change
Visible blood in urine or stool

faq.q: Why is splenectomy still used in ITP?
faq.a: The spleen is the main site of antibody‑mediated platelet destruction; removing it can produce durable remission in refractory cases.
In children, many cases are self‑limited and resolve within 6‑12 months; adults often need ongoing therapy.

faq.q: Is platelet transfusion effective in ITP?
faq.a: Only for life‑threatening bleeding; transfused platelets are rapidly destroyed by circulating antibodies.

exam: Describe the diagnostic criteria for ITP and how you would exclude other causes of thrombocytopenia.
Explain the first‑line management steps for a patient with platelet count 8 × 10⁹/L presenting with mucosal bleeding.
List three secondary conditions that can precipitate ITP in low‑resource settings and how their treatment influences ITP management.
